newsitem.title: USA: Iran envoy urges for U.N. Afghanistan conference.
newsitem.headline: Iran envoy urges for U.N. Afghanistan conference.

text.p: Iran's U.N. ambassador called in a newspaper article on Monday for a U.N.-sponsored conference on the conflict in Afghanistan in a move seen as suggesting Tehran might wish to negotiate with Washington on the issue.

The U.S. State Department reacted coolly to the Washington Post article by envoy Kamal Kharrazi, saying it saw no need to consult with Iran on the Afghan war, although it remained ready for a dialogue with Tehran under certain conditions.
"Iran supports the U.N. initiative to convene an international meeting of states concerned with Afghanistan in the near future as a first step," Kharrazi said.

Despite the purist Islamic creed of Afghanistan's Taleban movement, which captured Kabul in September, its successes have alarmed Tehran, which continues to support the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani.

Kharrazi said Afghans needed urgent international help to overcome the cycle of violence in their country, and said efforts by interested states, the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Conference were the "only viable approach."

The Iranian envoy attacked U.S. policies in Afghanistan and other states in the region, saying "Iran's efforts at conciliation for political settlement of disputes invariably have faced overt and covert U.S. sabotage."

Washington's real motive, he said, was to enforce a semblance of security in Afghanistan so that a proposed oil and gas pipeline from Central Asia to the Indian Ocean could go through Afghanistan and not through Iran.
Despite Kharrazi's anti-U.S. rhetoric, the Washington Post said in an editorial that his article "seeks to engage the United States in a negotiation over Afghanistan."

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said U.S. policy on Afghanistan was not directed against Iran, but that "we can get along and have an Afghan policy without talking to the Iranians every day."
"They make an offer to the United States on the op-ed pages of one of the American newspapers. That's a serious offer?" he added.

Spelling out what he said was standard U.S. policy, Burns said a U.S.-Iranian dialogue was "theoretically possible" but would need to address alleged Iranian efforts to acquire muclear weapons, alleged support for terrorism, and opposition to the Middle East peace process.

Kharrazi's article, published on the 17th anniversary of the seizure of the U.S. embassy in Iran by Moslem militants, followed a Tehran conference last week that called for an end to fighting in Afghanistan and for U.N.-backed peace talks.

The United States initially showed interest in starting a dialogue with Taleban, but later backed off when the movement failed to gain control of the whole country and drew hostile U.S. media coverage with Islamic restrictions on women.
Washington has said it supports efforts by U.N. envoy Norbert Holl to broker a ceasefire and start peace talks.
